# **Lake Bolshoye Morskoye****,**Protected lake in Nizhnekolymsky District, Sakha Republic, Russia.
Lake Bolshoye Morskoye is a large body of water in the northern Kolyma Lowland with an oval outline and no islands. The water remains shallow in most areas, making the lake relatively simple in its geography.
This lake and its surroundings received protected status to preserve the natural environment of the region. The designation reflects efforts to safeguard the wilderness and ecological systems of this remote area.
The name translates to Big Sea, reflecting how local communities understand this body of water within their landscape. This naming choice shows the importance of the lake to the region's identity.
The water freezes from late September until June, making the lake inaccessible during winter and early spring. Plan a visit only during the brief summer window when the ice has melted completely.
A river flows out of this lake and connects it to the broader river system of the region. This waterway reveals how the lake feeds into a larger network of flowing water.

Hydrology and Climate

Primarily fed by snow and rain, the lake has a catchment area of 382 km² and lies within the basin of the Bolshaya Chukochya River, a tributary of the Kolyma River system. No systematic depth measurements have been conducted, but the water body remains ice-covered from late September to early June due to the region's harsh Arctic climate. [[2]](#ref-2) The nearest settlement, Pokhodsk, is approximately 130 km southeast, underscoring the area's remoteness and limited human impact.

Bolshoye Morskoye supports a typical Arctic freshwater ecosystem, though detailed biodiversity studies are scarce. Pleistocene Park is a nature reserve in Nizhnekolymsky District, Russia, where large grazing animals live on fenced grassland. The terrain rolls across tundra along the Kolyma River with small lakes and low birches between the open fields.

Sergey Zimov founded the area in 1996 as a scientific experiment to bring back ice age grasslands. His son Nikita later took over management and expanded the animal populations with species from other parts of Siberia and North America.

Researchers here work to bring back the animal life from the last ice age and watch how plant eaters change the land around them. The research station hosts biologists and climate experts who study how grasslands can slow down the thawing of frozen ground.

Access requires special permission through the association and a multi-day journey to the remote region near the Arctic coast. The best time to visit is during the short summer when rivers are open and animals graze on the open meadows.

Yakutian horses dig through snow with their hooves in winter and eat the grass beneath just as their ancestors did thousands of years ago. The animals also trample moss layers which lets more sunlight reach the ground and helps plant life renew faster.
